concepts.definition: A recorded event or measurement. An observation can constrain explanations without identifying a unique cause.
A proposed explanation that makes a prediction. Distinguish what it predicts from what you have actually observed.
A comparison designed to distinguish predictions while keeping other relevant conditions stable.

chapters.title: A wet pavement is not a weather report
chapters.summary: Move from noticing a result to comparing explanations.

blocks.text: You walk outside and notice wet pavement. Rain is one hypothesis, but a sprinkler or street cleaner could produce the same observation. The visible result alone does not establish which event occurred. A useful next step is to ask what else each explanation predicts.

blocks.title: Observation, competing predictions, and a check
blocks.caption: Original schematic. The arrows mean “prompts the next reasoning step,” not “proves.”
blocks.alternative: Wet pavement prompts two rival explanations: rain and a sprinkler. Rain predicts widespread wetness; a sprinkler predicts localized wetness. Inspect nearby sheltered and unsheltered areas to compare those predictions.

nodes.label: Wet pavement
nodes.detail: This is the recorded observation, not a cause.

nodes.label: Sprinkler hypothesis
nodes.detail: Predicts wetness in the watered area.

nodes.label: Compare nearby areas
nodes.detail: A distinguishing observation can weaken one explanation.

steps.title: Record what happened
steps.explanation: Start with wet pavement; do not silently add rain to the observation.

steps.title: Keep rival explanations
steps.explanation: Both rain and a sprinkler can explain the initial result.

steps.title: Seek a discriminating observation
steps.explanation: Compare predicted patterns. A result may weaken a hypothesis without proving its rival.

blocks.title: Why did the plant droop?
blocks.problem: A plant droops. One explanation is too little water; another is damaged roots.
steps: Record moisture and root condition instead of assuming that drooping means drought.
Predict that adding water helps a thirsty plant but does not repair damaged roots.
Compare otherwise similar plants, if feasible, and record the conditions and outcome. Do not change light, soil, and water simultaneously if you want to attribute the result.
blocks.conclusion: A test is useful when its outcomes distinguish explanations. Even a successful intervention need not establish a single cause in every setting.

blocks.title: Explains is not the same as proves
blocks.text: If rain makes pavement wet, wet pavement does not logically prove rain. Other causes can produce the same result. Look for evidence that distinguishes hypotheses rather than only evidence compatible with your favorite one.

blocks.prompt: A room gets quieter after you close a window. What can you conclude, and what would you test next?
blocks.answer: Closing the window is associated with reduced noise in this observation. To test whether it caused the change, compare open and closed conditions while recording outside activity and other sound sources. Do not infer that every source of noise was outdoors.

outcomes.text: Distinguish an observation from an explanation and propose a discriminating test.

practice.prompt: You see wet pavement. Which claims stay within the evidence?

options.text: A sprinkler is a possible explanation.
options.explanation: It is a compatible hypothesis, not an established cause.

practice.explanation: Select statements supported by the observation, keeping possibilities separate from proof.

practice.prompt: Which actions make a comparison easier to interpret?

options.explanation: Reducing competing changes helps attribute differences.
That makes the cause of a difference ambiguous.

options.text: Write down predictions before inspecting the result.
options.explanation: This makes it harder to retrofit the prediction to the outcome.

practice.explanation: A controlled comparison exposes assumptions and makes rival predictions testable.
